question.problem: If ${f}^{′}(x)=-|x-5|,$ which of the following could be the graph of a continuous function $y=f(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
The graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ is the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/54c03ba5ea869394d9b3d35c64bb012a8c5f9917a5ebb96fd67994ace6a84d4f.png)

Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there is one critical point: 

$\,$ $x=5$ 

Also, we have the following: 

- If ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

- If ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,5)$ | $5$ | $(5,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{no extr.}$ | $↘$ |

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x):$

- First, we draw the critical point. We choose an arbitrary point on the vertical line $x=5,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/25d067dcff3b0cc4b88859a318023288a7c9786b5c73910f2addf3952680596b.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

- Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $↘$ on $(-\infty ,5)$ and on $(5,\infty )$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes up to the left of $x=5$ and goes down to the right of $x=5.$

- Furthermore, since ${f}^{′}(x)$ is increasing to the left of $x=5$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)>0$, and, since it is decreasing to the right of $x=5$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)<0.$ So, $x=5$ is an inflection point at which the curve $y=f(x)$ changes from concave up to concave down.

So, we can draw as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/b7b1e5915931501d881ba5efc1aaccb8af3a604ac397ac662d8bb7811659c17a.png)

- Finally, since we are told that our graph must be continuous, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/cb451ce921bb8bc56576545b4503bf3dd44bb1ee070466576437c2ce980dd017.png)

**Note:** The graph we obtained is not the only possible one. Any similar graph that's shifted vertically up or down could also be considered a possible $y=f(x).$
